html:
On the 200 BCE map, Papuan covers New Guinea and nearby islands, home to the Papuan peoples, who speak hundreds of languages not related to the Austronesian tongues around them.

People reached New Guinea at least 50,000 years ago, when it was joined to Australia by land. In the highlands they became some of the world's first farmers. At Kuk Swamp they were draining land and growing bananas, taro and sugarcane thousands of years before 200 BCE. See Papuan Neolithic farmers.

From about 1500 BCE Austronesian seafarers, the Lapita voyagers among them, settled along parts of the coast and nearby islands, and the two peoples mixed and traded. Inland valleys stayed divided among many small groups, which is why New Guinea still has more languages than almost anywhere else on earth; see Papuan languages. Later maps carry them on as Papuans, and today most live in Papua New Guinea and Indonesia.
sum: On the 200 BCE map, Papuan covers New Guinea and nearby islands, home to the Papuan peoples, who speak hundreds of languages not related to the Austronesian tongues around them.
